forces.title: Private hospitals boosting investment in diagnostic devices
forces.description: Private hospitals in Ireland are continuously investing in diagnostics, specialist services, and capacity expansion due to strong demand for elective procedures. This ongoing investment supports the growth of the Medical Devices & Equipment sector, particularly for diagnostic devices. The trend reflects long-term confidence in healthcare sector fundamentals, creating a favorable environment for manufacturers and suppliers of diagnostic equipment.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Healthcare Sector H1 2026 Insights and H2 2026 Outlook July 2026

forces.title: Increasing adoption of AI and digital tech in healthcare delivery
forces.description: Private hospitals in Ireland are significantly investing in AI and digital transformation, including electronic health records, remote monitoring, and automation technologies. This trend is framed by Ireland's AI for Care Strategy 2026-2030 and supports the embedding of digital health technologies and AI within healthcare delivery. This creates increased demand for AI-enabled diagnostic hardware and wearable medical hardware, which fall under IN060301.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Healthcare Sector H1 2026 Insights and H2 2026 Outlook July 2026

forces.title: Insurers expanding into digital diagnostics to streamline care
forces.description: Health insurers are increasingly integrating into the full healthcare value chain, driven by objectives to diversify revenue and enhance value propositions. A key strategy involves identifying issues early and guiding care through digital diagnostics and telemedicine. This strategic shift by payers could drive demand for advanced diagnostic devices (part of IN060301) as they seek to streamline care delivery and improve health outcomes.
forces.source_title: How Insurers Are Going End-to-End in Health Care

forces.title: MedTech shifting towards software-enabled value creation and recurring revenue
forces.description: The medtech industry is undergoing a structural shift where software is becoming a critical driver for differentiation, growth, and patient impact. As hardware categories mature and face price pressure, software enables new recurring revenue models (e.g., premium analytics, subscription services) and embeds devices within broader clinical workflows. This fundamentally changes the value proposition of medical devices and requires integrating regulated software, including SaMD, into digital ecosystems.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: AI advances improving software development productivity in MedTech
forces.description: Advances in AI are significantly enhancing software productivity across industries, with organizations seeing 30 to 70 percent gains in development efficiency. For medtech, this presents a crucial opportunity and imperative to leverage these gains while upholding stringent quality, safety, and regulatory compliance standards for Software as a Medical Device (SaMD). This accelerates the development of advanced medical devices and AI-enabled hardware.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: SaMD integration critical for clinical differentiation and digital ecosystems
forces.description: Value in medtech is increasingly created not by software alone, but by integrating regulated Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) into broader digital ecosystems. This integration supports workflow optimization, data aggregation, and recurring revenue models, with SaMD providing core clinical differentiation. Examples include AI modules for polyp detection or digital ecosystems integrating surgical video and AI insights, directly impacting the capabilities and market for IN060301.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: Regulatory burdens impede rapid MedTech software development and innovation
forces.description: Software development in medtech is constrained by established regulatory and quality standards, leading to phased approaches that extend timelines by 20-30% and increase costs. The high cost of errors, including delayed launches and regulatory penalties, forces organizations to spend 7-10% of sales on quality activities. This challenge in balancing speed with regulatory-grade quality for SaMD limits innovation for devices under IN060301.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: Escalating cybersecurity risks for connected and AI-enabled medical devices
forces.description: Cybersecurity is a growing critical concern for medtech, especially with the expansion of connected devices, digital ecosystems, and AI-enabled capabilities. Increased vulnerability to attacks necessitates robust cybersecurity requirements throughout the development lifecycle of Software as a Medical Device (SaMD). The rapid pace of AI-driven vulnerability discovery intensifies pressure on medtech organizations to continuously monitor and remediate software risks, impacting IN060301 products.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: Mismatched development timelines hinder SaMD-hardware integration
forces.description: Integrating Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) with hardware, while enabling faster innovation, poses a significant challenge for medtech organizations. Product development timelines and frameworks for software and hardware often differ, creating friction. Successfully bridging this capability gap to deliver SaMD at speed without compromising quality, and integrating it with physical medical devices (IN060301), is crucial for future growth but currently a major obstacle.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: MedTech faces talent shortage in digital and analytics expertise
forces.description: The medtech industry faces a structural challenge in attracting and retaining digital, technology, and analytics talent. Compared to other sectors, medtech is often perceived as less attractive, with a limited availability of key technical skills like application development. This talent gap hinders the modernization of software development functions and limits the industry's capacity for innovation in areas like AI-enabled diagnostic hardware and other advanced medical devices.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

viewpoints.title: Irish healthcare investment supports MedTech growth amid shifting care models
viewpoints.description: The Bank of Ireland's outlook for Ireland's healthcare sector is positive, driven by favorable demographics and continuous investment across various care settings, including private hospitals. This includes specific investments in diagnostics, specialist services, and new technologies like remote monitoring and AI-enabled solutions. This environment fosters sustained demand for medical devices, diagnostic equipment, and related technologies within IN060301.
viewpoints.source_title: Bank of Ireland Healthcare Sector H1 2026 Insights and H2 2026 Outlook July 2026

pnl_drivers.description: High regulatory and quality standards for medical devices and SaMD lead to significant expenditure (7-10% of sales) on testing, verification, and documentation, impacting profit margins and business cases.

market_sizing.methodology: MedTech organizations, on average, spend 7 to 10 percent of their sales revenue on quality-related activities, which includes extensive testing, verification, and documentation for software releases, particularly for Software as a Medical Device (SaMD).
market_sizing.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device
